cloze.text: The {{c1::preimplantation}} period is the {{c2::first week}} after conception.
The {{c1::embryonic}} period spans weeks {{c2::2 through 8}}.
The {{c1::fetal}} period runs from week {{c2::9}} through birth.
The first trimester includes the {{c1::preimplantation}} and {{c1::embryonic}} periods.
At {{c1::fertilization}} (day 0) sperm and egg unite to form a zygote with {{c2::46}} chromosomes in total — the {{c3::genetic blueprint}} is established.
The {{c1::zygote}} (days 1–3) undergoes mitosis (cleavage divisions); cleavage produces {{c2::identical}} cells.
The {{c1::morula}} (days 3–4) is a solid ball of {{c2::16–32}} cells; {{c3::cell differentiation}} begins at this stage.
The {{c1::blastocyst}} (days 5–6) is a hollow ball with an inner cell mass (the {{c2::embryoblast}}) and an outer {{c3::trophoblast}} layer.
cloze.extra: Dental relevance: the inner cell mass will become the embryo and form the dental tissues.

cloze.text: During {{c1::implantation}} (days 6–7) the blastocyst embeds into the uterine lining (the {{c2::endometrium}}), establishing the maternal–embryo connection for nourishment.
The {{c1::bilaminar}} disk (week 2) has two layers: the {{c2::epiblast}} (top) and the {{c3::hypoblast}} (bottom).
cloze.extra: Dental relevance: prepares for axis formation and germ layer differentiation.

cloze.text: The trilaminar disk (week 3) forms three germ layers. Dental relevance: {{c1::ectoderm}} forms enamel, while mesoderm and {{c2::neural crest}} form pulp, dentin, PDL and cementum.
In week 4, {{c1::embryonic folding}} turns the flat disk into a 3D cylindrical shape and {{c2::organogenesis}} begins; the face, palate and tongue begin forming.
From week 9 (fetus) organs grow and mature; the {{c1::permanent tooth buds}} form and {{c2::mineralization}} of enamel, dentin and cementum begins.
The {{c1::neural tube}} (future brain and spinal cord) begins forming in week {{c2::3}}.
The face begins to form in weeks {{c1::4–5}} (frontal process, {{c2::branchial arches}}).
Tooth development starts in weeks {{c1::6–7}} with initiation of the {{c2::dental lamina}}.
Palate development begins in weeks {{c1::6–9}} as the {{c2::lateral palatine processes}} form.
In week {{c1::8}} the {{c2::primary palate}} fuses with the lateral palatine processes.
cloze.extra: The book's timings for palatal fusion vary between pages (p.185: palatal shelves fuse in week 6; cleft palate weeks 8–12).

cloze.text: Tooth buds for the {{c1::permanent}} teeth begin forming in the {{c2::second}} trimester.
In the {{c1::third}} trimester further hard tissue formation (enamel, dentin) occurs.
After fertilization the zygote undergoes {{c1::mitosis}} (individual cell division) to produce more cells.
As the {{c1::blastocyst}} (hollow in the middle) keeps dividing, it travels down to the {{c2::uterus}}.
By the end of the {{c1::first week}} the blastocyst is embedded in the endometrium, the {{c2::innermost}} lining of the uterus.
The bilaminar disk is suspended between the {{c1::amniotic cavity}} (on top) and the {{c2::yolk sac}} (at the bottom).
Within the bilaminar disk the {{c1::primitive streak}} forms, which initiates creation of the trilaminar disk.
After the primitive streak forms, epiblast cells migrate between the layers to create a third, intermediate layer: the {{c1::mesoderm}}.
In the trilaminar disk the ectoderm comes from the {{c1::epiblast}} and the endoderm from the {{c2::hypoblast}}.
Germ-layer prefixes: ecto- = {{c1::outer / outside}}; meso- = {{c2::middle}}; endo- = {{c3::inner / within}}.
cloze.extra: Each germ layer is programmed to develop into specific tissues, organs and systems — knowing the derivatives is fundamental to organogenesis.

cloze.text: The {{c1::ectoderm}} is the outermost germ layer; it forms structures that interact with the external environment, such as the {{c2::epidermis}} and the {{c3::nervous system}}.
cloze.extra: In dentistry: the enamel and other inner parts of the teeth.

cloze.text: The {{c1::endoderm}} is the innermost germ layer; it forms the internal linings of the {{c2::respiratory}} passages and the {{c2::digestive}} tract (and associated organs).
The {{c1::mesoderm}} (middle layer, between ectoderm and endoderm) gives rise to connective tissues, muscles, bone and the {{c2::circulatory system}}.
Once the trilaminar disk forms, the disc has a {{c1::cephalic}} end (head) and a {{c2::caudal}} end (tail).
The ectoderm creates the {{c1::enamel organ}}, which gives rise to {{c2::ameloblasts}} (→ enamel).
The ectoderm produces {{c1::neural crest cells}} — specialized migratory cells.
Neural crest cells form the cartilage and bone of the {{c1::face and jaw}} (e.g., maxilla, mandible) and the {{c2::cranial nerves}} and ganglia.
cloze.extra: Neural crest cells also form odontoblasts (dentin), dental pulp, cementum, PDL and alveolar bone.

cloze.text: The ectoderm contributes to the pharyngeal arches and pouches, which give rise to the middle ear bones, the {{c1::thymus}}, portions of the tongue and the {{c2::parathyroid}} glands.
In the dental sac (dental follicle), {{c1::cementoblasts}} form cementum, {{c2::fibroblasts}} form the PDL, and {{c3::osteoblasts}} form alveolar bone.
Craniofacial mesenchyme forms the {{c1::facial bones}} (maxilla, mandible) plus cartilage, connective tissue and nerves of the head and neck.
The mesoderm contributes to general muscles, {{c1::blood vessels}} and connective tissue, and supports structures in the tongue, jaw and oral cavity.
The mesoderm assists (alongside neural crest cells) in forming the {{c1::pulp}} and {{c1::dentin}}.
The endoderm helps form structures like the {{c1::tongue}} and {{c2::glands}}.
During embryonic folding the disk expands and balloons into a {{c1::3D cylindrical}} shape.
Folding of the head, tail, transverse and lateral sides occurs through the {{c1::differential growth}} of tissues that merge.
By the end of the {{c1::embryonic}} period a recognizable individual has developed, and most organs and body systems have formed.
Most {{c1::congenital malformations}} happen during the embryonic period, as differentiation, morphodifferentiation and proliferation occur.
The fetal period (week 9 to birth) involves {{c1::maturation}} of existing structures and enlargement of the embryo into a fetus.
The {{c1::frontonasal}} process forms the forehead, bridge of the nose, nasal septum, medial & lateral nasal processes, primary palate and philtrum of the upper lip.
The 1st pharyngeal (mandibular) arch forms the maxilla and mandible, the {{c1::malleus}} and {{c1::incus}}, and {{c2::Meckel's}} cartilage.
Muscles from the 1st arch: muscles of {{c1::mastication}}, {{c2::mylohyoid}}, {{c3::anterior}} belly of the digastric, and the {{c4::tensor tympani}} and {{c4::tensor veli palatini}}.
The 1st pharyngeal arch forms the {{c1::anterior 2/3}} of the tongue.
The 2nd pharyngeal (hyoid) arch forms the muscles of {{c1::facial expression}}, the {{c2::stapes}} and {{c2::stapedius}}, the {{c3::styloid process}} and the {{c4::lesser}} horn of the hyoid.
The 2nd pharyngeal arch forms the {{c1::posterior}} belly of the digastric and the {{c2::stylohyoid}} muscle.
The 3rd pharyngeal arch forms the {{c1::stylopharyngeus}} muscle, the {{c2::greater}} horn of the hyoid and part of the posterior tongue.
The 4th pharyngeal arch forms the {{c1::laryngeal cartilages}}, the pharyngeal {{c2::constrictors}}, the {{c3::levator veli palatini}} and the {{c4::cricothyroid}}.
Besides the 3rd arch, the {{c1::4th}} arch also forms part of the posterior tongue; it also forms the {{c2::epiglottis}}.
Mandibular arch = 1st pharyngeal arch = 1st {{c1::branchial}} arch — the terms pharyngeal and branchial arch are used interchangeably.
cloze.extra: Don't be confused: all three names refer to the same structure.

cloze.text: The frontonasal process is a {{c1::midline}} swelling that forms above the {{c2::stomodeum}}; it arises from {{c3::ectoderm overlying the forebrain}}, not from the branchial arches.
The frontonasal process forms the {{c1::upper}} face; its nasal pits are surrounded by the {{c2::medial}} and {{c2::lateral}} nasal processes.
{{c1::Nasal placodes}} (ectodermal thickenings) appear bilaterally and invaginate to form {{c2::nasal pits}}.
The {{c1::medial}} nasal processes fuse in the midline to form the {{c2::philtrum}} (groove in the upper lip), the {{c3::primary palate}} (premaxilla) and the nasal septum.
cloze.extra: Improper fusion with the maxillary processes can result in cleft lip or cleft palate.

cloze.text: The {{c1::lateral}} nasal processes form the {{c2::alae}} (sides) of the nose.
The face and structures of the oral cavity develop during weeks {{c1::3 through 12}}.
Branchial arches are {{c1::bilateral}} swellings that appear {{c2::inferior}} to the stomodeum (the primitive mouth).
The 1st branchial arch divides into the {{c1::maxillary}} process (→ maxilla) and the {{c2::mandibular}} process (→ mandible).
The 2nd to 6th arches form the {{c1::neck}} area; no structure results from the {{c2::5th}} arch.

The middle face derives from the paired maxillary processes: nose (root to apex), center of the upper lip, {{c1::zygomatic}} bones, portions of the temporal bones, cheeks, the {{c2::secondary}} palate, and the maxillary {{c3::canines and posterior teeth}}.
cloze.extra: The book also lists the philtrum here, but elsewhere (pp.183–184) it says the philtrum comes from the frontonasal/medial nasal processes.

cloze.text: The lower face (paired mandibular processes) forms the mandible, the mandibular teeth, associated tissues and part of the {{c1::tongue}}.
The upper face (frontonasal process) includes the forehead, bridge of the nose, primary palate, nasal septum, nasal ({{c1::olfactory}}) pits and the lateral nasal processes (alae).
The {{c1::buccopharyngeal (oropharyngeal)}} membrane first separates the stomodeum from the {{c2::foregut}}; its disintegration forms the oral cavity opening.
The stomodeum is lined by {{c1::ectoderm}}, which becomes the {{c2::oral epithelium}}.
Beneath the oral epithelium general {{c1::mesoderm}} is present at first; during tooth development segments of it are replaced by {{c2::ectomesenchyme}}.
Ectomesenchyme is formed by {{c1::neural crest cells}} (ectoderm-derived) and migrates into the developing tooth region.
The {{c1::dental papilla}} derives from ectomesenchyme and forms the {{c2::odontoblasts}} (→ dentin) and the dental {{c3::pulp}}.
The {{c1::dental follicle}} (dental sac) forms cementum, the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone.
Enamel comes from {{c1::ectoderm}} (not ectomesenchyme); ameloblasts from the {{c2::inner enamel epithelium}} create enamel.
The hard palate develops from weeks {{c1::5 through 12}}.
The primary palate (premaxilla) makes up the {{c1::anterior 1/3}} of the hard palate and holds the {{c2::four maxillary incisors}}.
The secondary palate forms from two {{c1::palatal shelves}} (from the {{c2::maxillary}} process) that fuse in the {{c3::sixth}} week; it makes up the posterior {{c4::2/3}} of the hard palate.
cloze.extra: It contains the maxillary canines and posteriors.

cloze.text: Cleft lip is failure of the {{c1::maxillary}} processes to fuse with the {{c2::medial nasal}} process, during weeks {{c3::4–7}}.
Cleft lip occurs in about 1 in {{c1::1000}} births (with or without cleft palate) and is more common in {{c2::males}}.
Cleft lip is more often {{c1::unilateral}}, especially on the {{c2::left}} side.
Cleft lip and palate are the most common {{c1::congenital malformations}} in the United States; their etiology is {{c2::unknown}}.
Cleft palate is failure of the {{c1::palatal shelves}} to fuse together or with the {{c2::primary palate}}.
Cleft palate develops between weeks {{c1::8–12}}.
cloze.extra: The book says "8–12 weeks of the embryonic period", but the embryonic period ends at week 8 (p.180).

cloze.text: Cleft palate occurs in 1 in {{c1::2500}} live births and is more common in {{c2::females}}.
A {{c1::cleft (bifid) uvula}} — a minor cleft of the posterior soft palate — is the least severe form of cleft palate.
With cleft palate, malposition of the teeth and {{c1::mouth breathing}} are common; both are risk factors for {{c2::periodontal disease}}.
Nursing and feeding are complicated with cleft palate; an {{c1::obturator}} (dental appliance covering the cleft area) can be used to block the hole.

basic.front: After 1 week of cleavage the blastocyst has two layers. What does each do?
basic.back: Trophoblast = nutritive layer for the embryo; embryoblast = becomes the embryo

basic.front: Which germ layer is generally NOT directly involved in tooth formation?
basic.extra: The table on p.182 says the same: endoderm does not directly form tooth structures.

basic.back: No — it is a specialized tissue formed from neural crest cells (ectoderm-derived). It gives rise to dentin, pulp, PDL, cementum and the jaw bones.

basic.front: On the board, which is correct: dentin is formed by ectoderm, by neural crest cells, by ectomesenchyme, or by odontoblasts?
basic.back: All four are correct — they are links in the same developmental chain.
basic.extra: Board Alert: be flexible in your thinking.

basic.front: Cleft lip and cleft palate each increase the risk of which four problems?
basic.back: Oral infection, periodontal disease, dental caries and malnutrition

mcq.question: A pregnant patient asks when her baby is most vulnerable to major congenital malformations. Which period is correct?
mcq.explanation: Most congenital malformations happen in the embryonic period, while differentiation, morphodifferentiation and proliferation occur and most organs form. In the fetal period (C) existing structures mainly grow and mature.

mcq.question: Which dental tissue comes from ectoderm WITHOUT passing through ectomesenchyme?
mcq.explanation: Enamel is made by ameloblasts of the enamel organ, which comes straight from ectoderm (not ectomesenchyme). Dentin, pulp and cementum come from ectomesenchyme (neural crest) via the dental papilla and dental sac.

mcq.question: An infant is born without a thymus or parathyroid glands. Abnormal development of which structures is the most likely cause?
mcq.explanation: The pharyngeal arches and pouches give rise to the middle ear bones, thymus, parts of the tongue and the parathyroid glands. The primitive streak (D) starts the trilaminar disk, not specific glands.

mcq.question: A patient with Bell's palsy cannot move the muscles of facial expression on one side. These muscles develop from which pharyngeal arch?
mcq.explanation: The 2nd (hyoid) arch forms the muscles of facial expression. The 1st (mandibular) arch forms the muscles of mastication — the classic distractor.

mcq.question: All of the following derive from the 1st pharyngeal arch EXCEPT:
mcq.explanation: The stapes (and stapedius) come from the 2nd arch. The malleus and incus, Meckel's cartilage and tensor veli palatini all come from the 1st arch.

mcq.question: No adult structure results from which pharyngeal arch?
mcq.explanation: Arches 2–6 form the neck, but no structure comes from the 5th arch. The 4th arch forms the laryngeal cartilages, pharyngeal constrictors, levator veli palatini and cricothyroid.

mcq.question: Fusion of the medial nasal processes in the midline forms all of the following EXCEPT:
mcq.explanation: The alae (sides of the nose) come from the lateral nasal processes. The medial nasal processes form the philtrum, the primary palate (with the four maxillary incisors) and the nasal septum.

mcq.question: A child has a cleft palate that runs behind the incisive area, between the two palatal shelves. Which part of the palate failed to form normally, and where did it come from?
options: A. Primary palate — medial nasal process
mcq.explanation: The secondary palate (posterior 2/3 of the hard palate) forms when the two palatal shelves, which come from the maxillary process, fuse. The primary palate (A) is the anterior 1/3 and comes from the medial nasal process.

mcq.question: A newborn girl has a bifid uvula. Which statement is correct?
options: A. It is the most severe form of cleft lip
B. It is the least severe form of cleft palate
C. It is caused by failure of the maxillary and medial nasal processes to fuse
D. It is more common in males
mcq.answer: B. It is the least severe form of cleft palate
mcq.explanation: A cleft (bifid) uvula is a minor cleft of the posterior soft palate — the mildest form of cleft palate, which is more common in females. Failure of the maxillary and medial nasal processes to fuse (C) causes cleft lip.
